passages.title: About Lucy
passages.text: Hi! My name is Lucy. I am ten years old. I live in a small house with my mum, my dad and my brother, Sam. We have a dog called Max. Max is brown and white. I go to school by bus. My favourite subject is art.

passages.title: Notice in a cafe window
passages.text: GREEN CAFE. Open Monday to Saturday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Closed on Sunday. Coffee: $2. Tea: $1.50. Cake: $3. Free Wi-Fi for customers.

passages.title: An email to a friend
passages.text: Hi Anna, thank you for your invitation! I would love to come to your birthday party on Saturday. I work in a shop on Saturday mornings, but I finish at one o'clock. I can be at your house at about two. Shall I bring something? I can make a chocolate cake. See you on Saturday! Maria

passages.title: Weather forecast
passages.text: Tomorrow will be sunny in the south, with temperatures around 25 degrees. In the north it will be cloudy, and there will be some rain in the afternoon. On Thursday the rain will move to the south, and it will become colder everywhere.

passages.title: Learning a language abroad
passages.text: Many people believe that living abroad is the quickest way to learn a language. Tom, who moved to Spain two years ago, is not so sure. "At first I spent most of my time with other English speakers, so my Spanish stayed poor," he says. "Things changed when I joined a local football team. I had to talk to my teammates every week, and I learned much faster." Tom now advises language learners to find a hobby where they can meet local people.

passages.title: Library changes
passages.text: From next month, the city library will open one hour earlier, at 8 a.m., but it will close at 6 p.m. instead of 8 p.m. on weekdays. Weekend hours will not change. Members will be able to borrow up to ten books at a time instead of five. Late fees will rise from 10 to 20 cents a day.

passages.title: The rise of remote work
passages.text: Over the past decade, remote working has moved from being a rare perk to a common arrangement. Supporters argue that employees save time and money by avoiding the daily commute, and they often report being more productive at home. Critics, however, point out that working alone can lead to isolation, and that younger staff in particular miss the informal learning that happens in an office. As a result, a growing number of companies are choosing a hybrid model, in which employees work from home for part of the week and come into the office for the rest.

passages.title: A car-free town centre
passages.text: The city council's plan to ban cars from the town centre has divided residents. Shop owners fear that customers will go to out-of-town shopping centres if they cannot park nearby, while many parents welcome safer, cleaner streets for their children. The council insists that a free shuttle bus and extra cycle lanes will keep the centre accessible. A trial period of six months will begin in September, after which the council will review the results before making a final decision.

passages.title: Handwriting in the classroom
passages.text: Although handwriting has long been regarded as a fundamental skill, its place in the classroom is increasingly questioned. Proponents of typing argue that, in an era dominated by keyboards and touchscreens, the hours spent perfecting cursive could be better devoted to coding or critical thinking. Yet research complicates this view: studies suggest that students who take notes by hand tend to process information more deeply, since they cannot transcribe every word and are therefore forced to summarise. This does not necessarily mean that keyboards should be abandoned; rather, it implies that schools should be selective about when each tool is used.

passages.title: A redesigned museum wing
passages.text: When the museum unveiled its redesigned east wing, critics were quick to praise the architecture but less enthusiastic about the exhibits inside. "The building is a triumph," wrote one reviewer, "yet the displays seem to have been an afterthought." The museum's director has conceded that the criticism is partly justified, noting that the budget for the interior was cut in half during construction. She has promised that new galleries will be added over the next two years as additional funding is secured.

passages.title: The myth of steady scientific progress
passages.text: It is tempting to portray the history of science as a steady march towards truth, each generation building neatly upon the last. Historians of science, however, have long cautioned against this tidy narrative. Paradigm shifts, they note, seldom occur because older theories are conclusively disproved; more often, they succeed because their defenders retire or die, leaving a generation of researchers more receptive to unfamiliar ideas. Moreover, anomalies that later seem decisive were frequently dismissed at the time as experimental error. The implication is not that science is arbitrary, but that its progress is messier, and more dependent on human circumstance, than textbooks suggest.

passages.title: A divisive novel
passages.text: The novel's reception has been curiously bifurcated. Reviewers admire its formal audacity, since the story unfolds in reverse chronological order, yet ordinary readers often abandon it, finding the structure alienating rather than illuminating. The author, unperturbed, has remarked that a book which pleases everyone is probably saying nothing of consequence. Whether one regards this as admirable conviction or mere self-justification depends largely on how one judged the book in the first place.

questions.question: My sister ___ a teacher.
questions.explanation: With he, she, it or a singular noun, the verb 'to be' is 'is'.

questions.question: There ___ two apples on the table.
questions.explanation: 'Two apples' is plural, so we use 'There are'.

questions.question: ___ you like coffee?
questions.explanation: Present simple questions with 'you' start with 'Do'.

questions.question: I ___ breakfast at seven o'clock every day.
questions.explanation: For a daily habit with 'I' we use the present simple: 'I have'.

questions.question: We use a ___ to eat soup.
questions.explanation: A spoon is the tool normally used for eating soup.

questions.question: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, ___, Friday.
questions.explanation: Thursday comes between Wednesday and Friday.

questions.question: My mother's mother is my ___.
questions.explanation: The mother of your mother (or father) is your grandmother.

questions.question: My name ___ Anna.
questions.explanation: We use 'is' (or the short form 's) with 'my name'.

questions.question: Cows give us ___. It is a white drink and we put it in tea.
questions.explanation: Milk is the white drink that comes from cows.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Question word + do + subject + verb: 'Where do you live?'

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: We have a big green car.
questions.explanation: Adjectives of size come before colour: 'a big green car'.

questions.question: My father is a ___. He works in a school.
questions.explanation: Add -er to a verb to name the person who does it: teach, teacher.

questions.question: How old is Lucy?
questions.explanation: The text says: 'I am ten years old.'

questions.question: How does Lucy go to school?
questions.explanation: The text says: 'I go to school by bus.'

questions.question: Who is Max?
questions.explanation: 'We have a dog called Max.' Max is the family dog.

questions.question: When is the cafe closed?
questions.explanation: The notice says: 'Open Monday to Saturday ... Closed on Sunday.'

questions.question: How much is a cup of tea?
questions.explanation: The notice says: 'Tea: $1.50.'

questions.question: Yesterday we ___ to the cinema.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' needs the past simple. The past of 'go' is 'went'.

questions.question: Look! The children ___ in the garden.
questions.explanation: 'Look!' points to something happening now, so we use the present continuous.

questions.question: Which is ___ city in your country?
questions.explanation: To compare one city with all the others we use 'the' + superlative: 'the biggest'.

questions.question: You ___ smoke in the hospital. It is not allowed.
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a prohibition: it is not allowed.

questions.question: The train to London leaves from ___ 4.
questions.explanation: Trains leave from numbered platforms at a station.

questions.question: It's very cold today. Put on your ___.
questions.explanation: A scarf keeps your neck warm in cold weather; the other items are for hot, sunny days.

questions.question: I'd like to ___ a table for two at the restaurant tonight.
questions.explanation: To 'book' a table means to reserve it in advance.

questions.question: How ___ brothers and sisters do you have?
questions.explanation: Brothers and sisters are countable, so we ask 'How many'.

questions.question: She is afraid ___ dogs.
questions.explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by the preposition 'of'.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: What time does the film start?
questions.explanation: Question word + does + subject + base verb: 'What time does the film start?'

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: My brother is taller than me.
questions.explanation: A comparison uses adjective + -er + than: 'taller than me'.

questions.question: She sings very ___.
questions.explanation: An adverb that describes a verb is formed with -ly: beautiful, beautifully.

questions.question: What does Maria do on Saturday mornings?
questions.explanation: She writes: 'I work in a shop on Saturday mornings.'

questions.question: When will Maria arrive at Anna's house?
questions.explanation: She finishes work at one and says: 'I can be at your house at about two.'

questions.question: What does Maria offer to bring?
questions.explanation: She says: 'I can make a chocolate cake.'

questions.question: What will the weather be like in the north tomorrow?
answers: Cloudy, with rain in the afternoon
questions.correct_answer: Cloudy, with rain in the afternoon
questions.explanation: The forecast says that in the north it will be cloudy, with some rain in the afternoon.

questions.question: When will it become colder everywhere?
questions.explanation: 'On Thursday ... it will become colder everywhere.'

questions.question: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
questions.explanation: In a first conditional, the 'if' clause uses the present simple, not 'will'.

questions.question: I've lived in this town ___ 2015.
questions.explanation: We use 'since' with a point in time (2015) and 'for' with a period of time.

questions.question: The book ___ I bought yesterday is really interesting.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is the relative pronoun for things.

questions.question: This bridge ___ in 1990.
questions.explanation: The bridge did not build itself, so we need a passive. The past passive is 'was built'.

questions.question: I'm sorry I'm late. The traffic was terrible, so I ___ the bus.
questions.explanation: 'Miss the bus' means to arrive too late to catch it.

questions.question: Can I ___ your pen? I forgot mine.
questions.explanation: You borrow something from someone; the owner lends it to you.

questions.question: There was a long ___ at the supermarket, so I waited twenty minutes to pay.
questions.explanation: A queue is a line of people waiting for their turn.

questions.question: I wish I ___ more free time. I'm always busy.
questions.explanation: After 'wish' about a present situation we use the past simple: 'I wish I had'.

questions.question: She's very good ___ solving problems.
questions.explanation: The adjective 'good' takes 'at' before an activity: 'good at solving'.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: I have never been to Australia.
questions.explanation: In the present perfect, 'never' goes between 'have' and the past participle.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb.

questions.question: The company is looking for an ___ person to lead the new team.
questions.explanation: The adjective is 'experienced' (having a lot of experience).

questions.question: What problem did Tom have at first?
questions.explanation: He spent most of his time with other English speakers, so his Spanish stayed poor.

questions.question: What helped Tom to improve his Spanish?
questions.explanation: 'Things changed when I joined a local football team.'

questions.question: What does Tom advise language learners to do?
answers: Find a hobby with local people
questions.correct_answer: Find a hobby with local people
questions.explanation: The last sentence: find a hobby where they can meet local people.

questions.question: What will change on weekdays?
answers: The library will open earlier and close earlier
The library will open earlier and close later
The library will open later and close earlier
The opening hours will stay the same
questions.correct_answer: The library will open earlier and close earlier
questions.explanation: It will open at 8 a.m., one hour earlier, and close at 6 p.m. instead of 8 p.m.

questions.question: How many books will members be able to borrow after the change?
questions.explanation: The notice says members can borrow up to ten books instead of five.

questions.question: If I ___ about the problem earlier, I would have fixed it.
questions.explanation: A third conditional (unreal past) uses 'if' + past perfect.

questions.question: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
questions.explanation: The film started before we arrived, so we use the past perfect.

questions.question: She suggested ___ a taxi because it was raining.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by an -ing form (or a 'that' clause), not by 'to' + infinitive.

questions.question: He denied ___ the window.
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by an -ing form: 'He denied breaking the window.'

questions.question: Because of the economic crisis, many firms had to ___ staff.
questions.explanation: To 'lay off' workers means to end their employment, usually because there is not enough work.

questions.question: I can't ___ with his rude behaviour any longer.
questions.explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate something annoying.

questions.question: Her speech had a great ___ on the audience.
questions.explanation: 'Effect' is the noun (a result); 'affect' is a verb meaning to influence.

questions.question: She is not used ___ getting up early.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' + -ing means 'be accustomed to'.

questions.question: He apologised ___ being late.
questions.explanation: The verb 'apologise' is followed by 'for' before the reason.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: I wish I had listened to her advice.
questions.explanation: To express regret about the past, use 'wish' + past perfect.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: She asked me whether I had finished the report.
questions.explanation: In reported questions the word order is that of a statement, with a backshifted tense.

questions.question: The ___ of the new bridge took almost three years.
questions.explanation: The noun from 'construct' is 'construction'.

questions.question: According to supporters, what is one benefit of remote working?
questions.explanation: Supporters say employees save time and money by avoiding the daily commute.

questions.question: What concern do critics have about younger staff?
answers: They are less productive at home
They miss informal learning in the office
questions.correct_answer: They miss informal learning in the office
questions.explanation: Critics say younger staff miss the informal learning that happens in an office.

questions.question: What are a growing number of companies doing?
questions.explanation: A hybrid model means working from home part of the week and in the office the rest.

questions.question: Why are some shop owners against the plan?
answers: They think the shuttle bus will be too expensive
They fear customers will shop elsewhere
questions.correct_answer: They fear customers will shop elsewhere
questions.explanation: Shop owners fear customers will go to out-of-town shopping centres if they cannot park nearby.

questions.question: What will happen after the six-month trial?
answers: The council will examine the results before deciding
The shuttle bus will stop running
questions.correct_answer: The council will examine the results before deciding
questions.explanation: The council will review the results before making a final decision.

questions.question: Hardly ___ the building when the alarm went off.
questions.explanation: After 'Hardly' at the start of a sentence we invert the subject and auxiliary: 'Hardly had he entered ...'.

questions.question: The proposal, ___ details were kept secret, caused a lot of controversy.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: the proposal's details.

questions.question: ___ the weather improves, the match will be postponed.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. The other options either change the meaning or are ungrammatical here.

questions.question: It's high time we ___ a decision.
questions.explanation: 'It's high time' is followed by the past simple, referring to the present.

questions.question: The minister's remarks were deliberately ___, leaving journalists unsure what she really meant.
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means open to more than one interpretation; the other words mean clear or direct.

questions.question: After years of hard work, the scientist's theory was finally ___ when the experiment confirmed it.
questions.explanation: To be 'vindicated' is to be proved right after doubt or criticism.

questions.question: The two companies have agreed to ___ their resources to develop the technology.
questions.explanation: To 'pool' resources means to combine them for a shared purpose.

questions.question: Had I realised how difficult the course would be, I ___ never have enrolled.
questions.explanation: A mixed inverted conditional: 'Had I realised ..., I would never have enrolled.'

questions.question: The proposal was rejected on the ___ that it was too expensive.
questions.explanation: 'On the grounds that' introduces the reason for a decision.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: Under no circumstances should you share your password.
questions.explanation: A negative adverbial at the start of the sentence causes inversion: 'should you share'.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: Rarely have I seen such a well-organised event.
questions.explanation: After a negative adverb like 'Rarely', the auxiliary comes before the subject.

questions.question: His ___ to detail was remarkable.
questions.explanation: 'Attention to detail' is the usual noun from 'attend'.

questions.question: According to supporters of typing, what could replace the time spent on cursive?
questions.explanation: The time 'could be better devoted to coding or critical thinking'.

questions.question: Why might handwritten notes support learning?
answers: Students cannot record everything, so they have to summarise
Teachers give higher marks for them
questions.correct_answer: Students cannot record everything, so they have to summarise
questions.explanation: Writing by hand is slower, which forces students to summarise and so process the information more deeply.

questions.question: What conclusion does the writer reach?
answers: Keyboards should be banned from classrooms
Schools should choose carefully when to use each tool
Typing is less effective than writing
questions.correct_answer: Schools should choose carefully when to use each tool
questions.explanation: The writer says schools should be 'selective about when each tool is used'.

questions.question: What was the critics' main reaction to the new wing?
answers: They praised the building more than the exhibits
They praised the exhibits but not the building
questions.correct_answer: They praised the building more than the exhibits
questions.explanation: Critics praised the architecture but were less enthusiastic about the exhibits.

questions.question: What does the director say about the criticism?
answers: It is partly fair, because the interior budget was reduced
questions.correct_answer: It is partly fair, because the interior budget was reduced
questions.explanation: She concedes the criticism is partly justified and says the interior budget was cut in half.

questions.question: Such ___ the extent of the damage that the building had to be demolished.
questions.explanation: 'Such was the extent ...' is an inverted structure; 'extent' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

questions.question: Were it not ___ your help, we would have failed.
questions.explanation: 'Were it not for' + noun means 'if it had not been for'.

questions.question: She is said ___ the manuscript before she died.
questions.explanation: For an action that happened before the time of reporting, use 'is said to have' + past participle.

questions.question: The committee insisted that the report ___ revised before publication.
questions.explanation: After verbs like 'insist' or 'demand' the subjunctive uses the base form: 'be revised'.

questions.question: The politician's ___ speech failed to address any of the concerns that voters had raised.
questions.explanation: 'Vapid' means lacking substance or interest.

questions.question: His ___ remarks about his colleagues eventually cost him his job.
questions.explanation: 'Disparaging' remarks express a low opinion of someone.

questions.question: The negotiations reached an ___, with neither side willing to compromise.
questions.explanation: An 'impasse' is a deadlock where no progress is possible.

questions.question: Not until the meeting had ended ___ I realise my mistake.
questions.explanation: 'Not until' at the start of a clause requires inversion: 'did I realise'.

questions.question: By and ___, people get used to new technology fairly quickly.
questions.explanation: 'By and large' is a fixed expression meaning 'in general'.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: Little did they suspect that the plan would fail.
questions.explanation: 'Little' used as a negative adverb at the start causes inversion: 'Little did they suspect'.

questions.question: Put the words in the correct order.
questions.correct_answer: Only then did the scale become clear.
questions.explanation: 'Only then' at the start of a sentence is followed by inversion: 'did the scale become'.

questions.question: Despite repeated requests, he showed a complete ___ to cooperate.
questions.explanation: Despite repeated requests, the sense is negative: un- + willing + -ness = 'unwillingness'.

questions.question: What do historians of science caution against?
answers: Believing that science has made no progress
Seeing scientific history as a neat, steady progression
questions.correct_answer: Seeing scientific history as a neat, steady progression
questions.explanation: They caution against 'this tidy narrative' of a steady march towards truth.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do new paradigms often succeed?
answers: Supporters of the old theories are replaced by researchers more open to new ideas
questions.correct_answer: Supporters of the old theories are replaced by researchers more open to new ideas
questions.explanation: New paradigms succeed more often because their defenders retire or die, leaving more receptive researchers.

questions.question: What is the writer's overall position?
answers: Science does progress, but less tidily than is often claimed
Textbooks describe the history of science accurately
questions.correct_answer: Science does progress, but less tidily than is often claimed
questions.explanation: The writer says science is not arbitrary, but its progress is messier than textbooks suggest.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the reception of the novel?
answers: Divided between reviewers and ordinary readers
questions.correct_answer: Divided between reviewers and ordinary readers
questions.explanation: 'Bifurcated' means divided in two: reviewers admire the novel, but ordinary readers often abandon it.

questions.question: What does the final sentence imply?
answers: How we judge the author's remark depends on our opinion of the book
The author is certainly justifying a failure
The author's view is clearly admirable
questions.correct_answer: How we judge the author's remark depends on our opinion of the book
questions.explanation: The writer says the verdict on the author's remark depends on how one judged the book in the first place.
